L70: ## About this ebook
L71: 
L72: An original methodological framework for approaching the archived web, both as a source and as an object of study in its own right.
L73: As life continues to move online, the web becomes increasingly important as a source for understanding the past. But historians have yet to formulate a methodology for approaching the archived web as a source of study. How should the history of the present be written? In this book, Niels Brügger offers an original methodological framework for approaching the web of the past, both as a source and as an object of study in its own right.
L74: While many studies of the web focus solely on its use and users, Brügger approaches the archived web as a semiotic, textual system in order to offer the first book-length treatment of its scholarly use. While the various forms of the archived web can challenge researchers' interactions with it, they also present a range of possibilities for interpretation.
L75: The Archived Web identifies characteristics of the online web that are significant now for scholars, investigates how the online web became the archived web, and explores how the particular digitality of the archived web can affect a historian's research process. Brügger offers suggestions for how to translate traditional historiographic methods for the study of the archived web, focusing on provenance, creating an overview of the archived material, evaluating versions, and citing the material.
L76: The Archived Web lays the foundations for doing web history in the digital age, offering important and timely guidance for today's media scholars and tomorrow's historians.

L562: The third section, cite310†‘Archives and Access’ , explores the long, intertwined existence between archives and historians with special focus on digital technology and source mediation. Historians are expert users of archives, although growing estrangement has led scholars increasingly to consider the interactions between the two parties as ‘interdisciplinary’ encounters.cite350†Footnote ^{14} This section thus explores how technology has changed the relationship between historian, archivist, and archives.
L563: What has the impact of partial collection digitization been? Online finding aids? Digital photography? Over the last two decades, historians are spending less time than ever before in archives, yet never have we had such powerful tools and platforms at our disposal.
L564: The fourth section, ‘Publishing in an Interdisciplinary Age: From Journal to Social Media’, explores the changing relationship between historians and their audiences. When historians think of ‘digital history’, many think of digital public history, thanks to the historical profession’s long lineage of public-facing engagement.cite351†Footnote ^{15} Public scholarship has taken the shape of CD-ROMs, exhibit sites, ‘memory banks’, social media, and engagement on Wikipedia.
L565: Yet traditional career progression – hiring, and in North America, tenure and promotion – compel scholars towards traditional markers of career success as embodied in certain publication types (especially traditional books). How has technology changed publishing? This section briefly explores new formats, the changing approaches towards idea circulation, and the potential for interdisciplinary engagement.
L566: Historians have rarely been transparent enough about many of the above topics: we treat scholarship as finished products, and methods are too often relegated to footnotes or informal discussions.cite352†Footnote ^{16} We could all do better history by reflecting on the ongoing technological transformation that is changing how we research.
L567: #### 1.3 Are We All Digital Historians Now? Digital History and the Digital Humanities
L568: Scholars have been exploring how to explicitly use new and emerging technologies for humanistic and historical research since the 1950s and 1960s, under the auspices of what we today call the Digital Humanities or more specifically Digital History. The relationship between these two DHs is complicated. Digital History owes its lineage both to the Digital Humanities and also to currents and trends within the broader historical profession, particularly public history.
L569: The Digital Humanities, broadly defined, explore the intersection of technology and the humanities.cite353†Footnote ^{17} In many ways, as Adam Crymble has explored at length, the Digital Humanities grows out of a digital literary studies tradition (by way of the Text Encoding Initiative and humanities computing scholars).cite354†Footnote ^{18} Historians have traditionally been underrepresented within the broad scope of the Digital Humanities and its earlier intellectual approaches.cite355†Footnote ^{19} L570: Digital History can be expansively defined as the intersection of historical scholarship with new and emerging technology. In practice, this can be broken into two subfields. First, some Digital Historians use technology to reach new and different audiences with new media, continuing a lineage of historians using new media to carry out the mission of social and public history.
L571: An understanding of the democratizing potential of technology has been foundational to this approach.cite356†Footnote ^{20} Secondly, other Digital Historians have used technology to do historical scholarship.cite357†Footnote ^{21} These scholars in part emerged from earlier approaches to quantitative history and historical demography – Social Science historians – as well as a smaller group of historians influenced by the more literary-focused computational studies approaches.cite358†Footnote ^{22} L572: Today, Digital Historians engage in a wide variety of scholarship. They may write programs or leverage computational platforms to assemble sources en masse, such as from records housed at the Internet Archive or the Library of Congress.
L573: Data are analysed by extracting features (i.e., word frequency, detected items in images, place names) before being subsequently analysed and visualized in a variety of ways.cite359†Footnote ^{23} Other Digital Historians challenge conventional norms of scholarship, exploring new methods of scholarly communication. While it is impossible to do justice to this field in a few sentences, it is a vibrant subfield adopting explicit new methodologies and approaches.
L574: Yet what about other historians who use computers to do their work but who do not fall into the above categories? Historians now all use databases, run keyword searches across millions of documents, and take digital cameras to turn scholarly documents into electronic files to be analysed at home. Are we now all digital historians?
L575: There is a fruitful distinction to be made between Digital History – the delineated field of study bounded by academic journals, conferences, and pedagogical approaches – and ‘digitized history’, or the broader transformation prompted by technology. We are not all Digital Historians (my capitalization is deliberate). But we all engage with digitized sources and workflows. It is unwise to silo historical engagement with technology as a subfield given its sweeping impact on the entire profession.
L576: A focus on Digital History can make the rest of the historical profession think that ‘we are not digital historians’, as they fire up their web browsers and research over the Internet. We are all digital now.
L577: #### 1.4 The Digitally Aware Historian
L578: 
L579: Let me close this introduction on an optimistic note by imagining a digitally aware historian who takes the content of this Element to heart. What kind of work would a historian who was fully cognizant of the work that technology was playing in mediating their work do?
L580: They begin to research their topic in a newspaper database. But rather than haphazard keyword searches, they instead look at which newspapers and years are included in the database – and which ones are not. They then explicitly consider selection bias (why was this newspaper digitized but not that one) and do some contextual research on the period’s newspapers.
L581: Perhaps at the end of the day they believe that the accessible advantages of the digitized newspapers outweigh the limitations of their selectivity bias, and accordingly write a few sentences to that effect in their introduction. This sets the tone for their engagement with sources throughout their manuscript. The historian thinks about what is present and what is missing.
L582: For an event, they go page-by-page for a few weeks before and after the event, developing a contextual sense of the source as well as to ensure that the OCR has not missed salient keywords. Scholarship is still assisted by databases, but every step is deliberate and thoughtful. When a button in the interface is clicked, it is done so deliberately. The database is no longer a black box.
L583: The time then comes to work with other digitized primary sources, and many of the same questions come to the historian’s mind: what’s there? What’s not there? They respectfully email an archival colleague and ask these questions. The sources that are used are deliberately framed and contextualized. They understand their sources and are self-reflective about their use.
L584: The historian then goes to the archive. They anticipate a follow-up archival trip, to follow theoretical rabbit holes that will inevitably arise when looking through their digitized photographs at home after their trip. As they leave the archive, they offer to share photographs with the archive as well in case it might help. After finishing their research, they tweet about their work, think about primary sources, and are transparent in their writing about argument, method, and approach.
L585: Maybe they will become a Digital Historian. This could entail adopting new analytical lenses, moving away from the typical approach of ‘close reading’ to one of distant reading. Alternatively, they could draw on metadata to visualize interconnections between sources, or challenge norms of scholarship by publishing a database, a map, or another novel form of scholarly communication. New frontiers may then present themselves. But most historians will not go down this route.
L586: Instead, what we have seen in the above hypothetical of a digitally conscious researcher is one that pays heed to the mediating influence of technology on their work. The researcher understands that the way by which sources are mediated has had profound impact on how they are read, understood, and contextualized. In short, this is a digitally-aware historian, actively using technology rather than being shaped by it.

L197@P15-19: For that reason, at the end of the day, this work is for him.HISTORY IN THE AGE OF ABUNDANCE?INTRODUCTION
L198@P19: Our collective cultural heritage, the legacy that we leave behind for
L199@P19: the generations to come, faces a serious problem in the digital age. We
L200@P19: used to, as a rule, forget. Now we have the power of recall and retrieval
L201@P19: at a scale that will decisively change how our society remembers. For
L202@P19: historians, professionals who interpret and bring shape to narratives
L203@P19: of the past, this is a dramatic shift. The digital age brings with it great
L204@P19: power: the prospect of a more democratic history and of more voices
L205@P19: included in the historical record, a realization of the social historian’s
L206@P19: dream. Yet it also brings significant challenges: what does it mean to
L207@P19: write histories with born-digital sources – from websites written in the
L208@P19: mid-1990s to tweets posted today? How can we be ready, from a technical perspective as well as from a social or ethical one, to use the web
L209@P19: as a historical source – as an archive? Historians with the training and
L210@P19: resources are about to have far more primary sources, and the ability to
L211@P19: process them, at their fingertips. What will this all mean for our understanding of the past? How can these sources be used responsibly? Finally,
L212@P19: if historians cannot rise to the moment, what does this mean for the
L213@P19: future of our profession?
L214@P19: The problem can be summed up in something as innocuous as a
L215@P19: personal homepage, hosted on the free GeoCities.com service. GeoCities.
L216@P19: com, founded in 1994, provided free websites to anybody who wanted
L217@P19: to create one. A user would visit GeoCities.com, enter an email address,
L218@P19: and receive a free megabyte (later two, then ten) to stake an individual
L219@P19: space on the burgeoning Information Superhighway. These sites took
L220@P19: many shapes and sizes: a Buffy the Vampire Slayer fan site, a celebration
L221@P19: of a favourite sports team, a family tree, even a young child’s tribute to
L222@P19-20: Winnie the Pooh. Early web users flocked. By October 1995, the first 4 History in the Age of Abundance?
L223@P20: ten thousand users had created their sites. Two years later, a million
L224@P20: had. And by 2009, some seven million users had created accounts on
L225@P20: GeoCities.com. While just how to define a webpage itself is a complicated question – as we explore in this book, a webpage is really a
L226@P20: collection of resources and files (from text, images, embedded widgets,
L227@P20: movies, to style sheets, or other interactive components) that are pulled
L228@P20: together by your web browser – it is clear that these 7 million accounts
L229@P20: are emblematic of the growing scale of web archives. Indeed, if we count
L230@P20: these unique webpages, we see that there were over 186 million of them.
L231@P20: Yet if you visit GeoCities.com today, you will see only an advertisement
L232@P20: for one of Yahoo!’s website hosting services – no evidence at all of the
L233@P20: human activity that had once happened there. Without web archiving,
L234@P20: these websites would have been, for the most part, irretrievably lost.
L235@P20: Thanks to the Internet Archive, however, we can today “visit”
L236@P20: GeoCities. The San Francisco–based Internet Archive, founded in April
L237@P20: 1996 by Brewster Kahle and Bruce Gilliat, grew out of a recognition
L238@P20: that people were increasingly living their lives online and that this
L239@P20: culture was in danger.1 Legally designated a library in 2007 by the State
L240@P20: of California, the non-profit Internet Archive now has expansive holdings, including hundreds of billions of webpages, millions of books,
L241@P20: audio recordings, videos, and images, and over a hundred thousand
L242@P20: software programs, all freely accessible at http://archive.org.
L243@P20: 2
L244@P20:  When you
L245@P20: go to the Internet Archive’s website and access one of their archived
L246@P20: websites, you are accessing data stored on a hard drive within their
L247@P20: repurposed Christian Science church in San Francisco’s Richmond
L248@P20: District (see figure i.1).
L249@P20: In many ways, the founding of the Internet Archive in 1996 was
L250@P20: a visionary act. The library was a critical reaction to the fact that our
L251@P20: society was undergoing a medium shift in how we document our lives,
L252@P20: societies, and cultures. As the West rapidly transitioned from traditional
L253@P20: print sources, which we had preservation strategies for, towards digital
L254@P20: bits and bytes, the transitory nature of websites and content opened up
L255@P20: an opportunity for the Internet Archive to help preserve our cultural
L256@P20: memory. The Archive does so in part by collecting the world’s largest
L257@P20: web archive, the generic term for the collections of web content for
L258@P20: use by present and future historians, researchers, and even members of
L259@P20: the public; web archiving is the process of gathering, storing, preserving, and making accessible that data.3
L260@P20-21:  As we collectively move online, Introduction 5
L261@P21: we also produce far fewer traditional paper records than we did before,
L262@P21: making this preservation process increasingly indispensable.
L263@P21: You can visit the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine at http://
L264@P21: archive.org/web and “go back in time” to visit the rudimentary, often
L265@P21: broken, archived copies of personal (or corporate, or educational, or
L266@P21: beyond) websites collected between 1996 and 2009. The Wayback
L267@P21: Machine – the name comes from Sherman and Mr Peabody’s “WABAC
L268@P21: machine” from the Rocky and Bullwinkle Show – is the Internet Archive’s
L269@P21: portal to let you access their collections. Try it yourself by visiting the
L270@P21: Wayback Machine and searching for http://GeoCities.com. In the case
L271@P21: of GeoCities, it offers over 186 million distinct web addresses, some
L272@P21: 32 billion words to index, search, and explore. This information is now
L273@P21: at the fingertips of anybody with an internet connection and a web
L274@P21: browser, to remotely access and explore information held on those hard
L275@P21: drives in California. That the voices of so many could conceivably reside
L276@P21: on a (big) hard drive speaks volumes about how the historical record
L277@P21: is dramatically changing. GeoCities exemplifies the shifting scope of
